editorial:
Imagine being Abraham Lincoln, leading a country through a brutal war, only to lose your youngest son. You are dealing with a pain that feels impossible to carry. This story takes you inside a graveyard where the lines between life and death are blurred. You get to see Lincoln visiting his son's crypt, but you are not alone. A crowd of ghosts surrounds him, all stuck in a middle place called the Bardo. They talk and argue about their own lives while watching this father grieve. It feels more like a play than a standard movie, with a very strange and artistic vibe that pulls you into a dreamlike state.

The acting is top notch, and the way the ghosts interact keeps things interesting even when the plot slows down. You might find the slow pace a bit weird at first, but it helps you feel the sadness of the characters. If you enjoy stories that focus on feelings rather than big explosions, you will love this.
endingExplained: At the end, the ghosts finally realize they cannot stay in the Bardo forever. They have to stop clinging to their old regrets and move on to the next life. You see them accept their deaths and fade away peacefully. Lincoln also finds a way to cope with his loss, knowing his son is finally at peace. The movie wraps up by showing that love is the only thing that lasts after we are gone.
targetAudience: Ideal for anyone who loves historical dramas and artistic storytelling.
